01 / Introduction

Introduction and research scope

A systematic strategy is a specified decision process: what information it observes, how it forms positions, how those positions are traded and how their economic results are measured.

The previous Quant Basics projects explained instrument valuation, simulation, portfolio construction and tail risk. This project connects those tools to a trading process that evolves over time. Its central object is a reproducible strategy specification, rather than a fitted curve that happens to rise in a historical chart.

A strategy combines a hypothesis about returns with a rule for acting on that hypothesis. A signal alone is incomplete: execution delay, exposure, cash returns, costs, financing, risk limits and evaluation design can materially change the result. A seemingly minor time-indexing error can give a strategy information that was unavailable when its trade would have occurred.

An analogy: an experiment and its laboratory notebook

A trading idea resembles an experimental hypothesis. The strategy specification is the protocol, the backtest is an experiment under recorded assumptions, and the research log records every alteration. Rewriting the protocol after seeing the outcomes changes what the experiment can establish. A reproducible notebook makes that distinction visible.

What this guide develops

Part I establishes economic hypotheses, information timing, data, signals and sizing. Part II develops portfolio mechanics, trading costs, execution, account reconciliation and evaluation. Part III covers performance, statistical uncertainty, robustness, capacity and an interactive laboratory. Mathematical notation accompanies each layer, and worked examples connect the formulas to actual account movements.

The main teaching strategy is a single-asset long/cash rule. It chooses a risky exposure from trailing price information, optionally scales that exposure by estimated volatility and executes after an explicit delay. A contrarian rule provides a comparison. These simple examples keep accounting transparent; the same research principles extend to multiple assets, long/short portfolios and more complex forecasting models.

All price paths, numerical strategy outcomes and selection experiments on this page are synthetic. Their generating assumptions are stated. Synthetic data allow the mechanics to be inspected and independently tested; they do not establish that a trading rule has an exploitable edge in a real market. The offline laboratory lets you change a rule and immediately observe its mechanical consequences.

Prerequisites

Simple and log returns, expectations, variance and elementary statistics are sufficient for most chapters. Portfolio notation uses vectors. Statistical inference introduces serial dependence and multiple testing. Knowledge of a programming language helps with the appendix, but the account examples can be followed with a calculator.

The aim is to learn how to formulate and evaluate a strategy honestly. A clear null hypothesis, explicit benchmark and complete cash ledger are as important as an elaborate signal. More sophisticated modeling can refine the process after those foundations are correct.

02 / Research design

Economic hypotheses and strategy specifications

Begin by stating why a signal might predict a return or compensate an investor for taking a risk. Candidate mechanisms include delayed information response, risk premia, institutional constraints, liquidity provision or temporary order-flow pressure. A rule found by searching many transformations without a hypothesis may still be interesting, but its statistical evidence must account for that search.

A strategy specification should state its universe, data timestamps, feature definition, forecast horizon, position map, rebalance schedule, execution convention, cost model and benchmark. Write it in a form that two independent implementations can reproduce. “Buy when momentum is strong” is ambiguous; “after close tt, form a target using the sign of the last 63-session return, submit it for close t+1t+1, and hold the filled exposure over the next interval” is testable.

S=(U,I,g,h,E,C,R),st=g(It),wttarget=h(st,It).\mathcal S=(\mathcal U,\mathcal I,g,h,\mathcal E,\mathcal C,\mathcal R),\qquad s_t=g(\mathcal I_t),\quad w_t^{\mathrm{target}}=h(s_t,\mathcal I_t).
(01)

Here U\mathcal U is the universe, It\mathcal I_t the available information, gg the signal function, hh the exposure map, E\mathcal E execution, C\mathcal C costs and R\mathcal R risk controls. The notation emphasizes that the signal is only one part of the system.

Predictability, compensation and implementation

A positive average return can come from ordinary market exposure rather than forecasting skill. A strategy that stays long most of the time may earn an equity premium even if its timing adds no value. Compare it with relevant exposure and cash benchmarks. A long/short relative-value strategy needs a different benchmark from a long/cash allocation rule.

A statistically detectable effect may be too small to trade after costs. Conversely, an economic exposure may be useful in a portfolio even if its standalone Sharpe ratio is modest. State the intended role: return generation, diversification, hedging, liquidity provision or dynamic allocation. Success criteria should reflect that role.

Precommitment and an experiment log

Before evaluating a candidate, define the sample split, primary metric, cost assumptions and rejection conditions. Record variants, failed ideas and revisions. A researcher who examines 100 strategies and reports only the best has conducted a different experiment from someone who tested one pre-specified rule.

Separate a discovery stage from confirmatory evaluation. Exploratory plots help identify mechanisms and coding mistakes, but should not be relabeled as untouched evidence. A final evaluation period becomes development data once its results influence the model. Paper trading supplies additional forward observations while testing operational assumptions.

Define a falsifiable implication. A mean-reversion idea should specify when, how quickly and under which market conditions deviations are expected to reverse. A vague story that explains every possible result cannot distinguish a working model from a narrative attached after the fact.

03 / Causality

Information sets and execution timing

Let Ft\mathcal F_t represent information available after time tt. A valid forecast or formation signal is measurable with respect to that information. It cannot depend on a price, a revised economic release or an instrument membership decision that becomes known later.

st=g(Ft),Rt+1=Pt+1Pt−1.s_t=g(\mathcal F_t),\qquad R_{t+1}=\frac{P_{t+1}}{P_t}-1.
(02)

A simple pedagogical return equation uses a position known at the interval's start: Rp,t+1=wtRt+1R_{p,t+1}=w_tR_{t+1}. But if wtw_t depends on the finalized close PtP_t, executing exactly at that same close requires a realistic closing-auction information and order-submission model. Merely shifting a return series by one row does not settle this operational question.

The convention used on this page

The laboratory uses a full-session execution delay by default. A target formed after close kk is executed at close k+1k+1. It first earns the close-to-close return ending on day k+2k+2. For a general delay d≥1d\ge1, the target used for return period jj comes from formation close:

k=j−1−d,wj=wktarget.k=j-1-d,\qquad w_j=w_k^{\mathrm{target}}.
(03)

The account is rebalanced at price Pj−1P_{j-1}, after the target has been known for dd sessions, then held to PjP_j. Costs are deducted at the rebalance. The prices are synthetic closing observations with assumed guaranteed fills; real auction execution needs additional modeling. This convention is intentionally explicit so that every ledger row can be traced to its information date.

Common timing errors

Selecting today's position with today's realized return creates a profitable-looking selector that could only be known after the trade. Centered moving averages include future observations. A volatility estimate calculated over the full sample uses future scale information. Choosing a parameter on an evaluation block and then applying it to the start of that same block leaks the block's outcomes.

Economic releases have publication and revision timestamps in addition to reference periods. A month-end value published weeks later was not available at month end. Use point-in-time versions when the strategy depends on real-time fundamentals. For machine learning, a label may extend into the future even when its feature row has an earlier timestamp.

A causality test

Compute all features and executed positions up to date tt. Replace every observation after tt with a different future path. The earlier features and decisions should remain unchanged. This suffix-perturbation test catches many accidental future dependencies. It does not by itself verify data vintages or fill realism, which require their own checks.

The right timing is a property of the entire pipeline. Formation, order release, execution, financing and attribution each have timestamps. Saving these in an event ledger turns a vague assurance of “no look-ahead” into something that can be inspected.

04 / Data

Market data and point-in-time universes

Data define the experiment's observable market. Identify price type, currency, timestamp, calendar, instrument identifier and adjustment policy. A closing trade, midpoint, settlement price and indicative quote are different observations. Their suitability depends on the proposed execution and valuation conventions.

Corporate actions and investable prices

Splits change share counts and nominal prices; dividends transfer value from the company to the cash account. A total-return series can model reinvested wealth, while a raw price series plus explicit corporate-action cash flows can support a detailed holdings ledger. Mixing adjusted prices with separate dividend credits double counts the distribution.

A historical adjustment may use information learned later. That does not automatically invalidate a return series for every purpose, but feature interpretation matters. A split-adjusted price threshold designed to mimic an absolute market price can change retrospectively. Store raw data, adjustment factors and the intended feature convention.

Universe membership and missing observations

A present-day list of surviving equities excludes companies that disappeared. Testing past dates only on that list introduces survivorship bias. A historical universe should use membership and tradability known at each date, including delistings and their economic outcomes. Removing an instrument because its later history looks problematic conditions the past selection on future information.

Missing data are not always random. A suspension, stale quote or market closure can carry economic information. Forward-filling a price may be appropriate for a valuation mark but does not imply that a trade could have filled there. Align markets carefully: different closing times can create spurious relationships when returns are treated as simultaneous.

The synthetic dataset

This guide uses 1,512 synthetic sessions with initial price 100 and five artificial regimes. Each log return has a regime-specific drift, an AR(1) term and normal innovation. The regimes divide the sample into five equal-length blocks; they are part of the data generator, not signals revealed to the strategy.

gj=ma(j)+φa(j)gj−1+σa(j)Zj,Pj=Pj−1egj,Zj∼N(0,1).g_j=m_{a(j)}+\phi_{a(j)}g_{j-1}+\sigma_{a(j)}Z_j,\qquad P_j=P_{j-1}e^{g_j},\quad Z_j\sim N(0,1).
(04)

The generator is reproducible from its seed and uses no external market data. Prices remain positive. Changing the seed changes the observations while retaining the chosen data-generating model. A simulated trend regime can make a trend rule look effective by construction; the experiment demonstrates conditional mechanics, not a universal trading result.

For real research, keep a data manifest with source, download time, revision policy and transformation steps. Reproducibility requires the exact input dataset, not merely the name of a vendor whose history may later be corrected.

05 / Return measurement

Returns, compounding and benchmarks

Simple returns measure proportional changes in wealth or price. Log returns provide additive time aggregation when prices are positive:

Rt=PtPt−1−1,gt=ln(1+Rt),PTP0=∏t=1T(1+Rt)=e∑tgt.R_t=\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}-1,\qquad g_t=\ln(1+R_t),\qquad \frac{P_T}{P_0}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1+R_t)=e^{\sum_tg_t}.
(05)

A portfolio of initial capital weights combines simple asset returns linearly over one period when the holdings and cash flows match that model. Log returns generally do not aggregate linearly across assets. They are useful for time-series modeling but should be converted back to prices or simple returns for an exact cash account.

A +10% return followed by a −10% return multiplies wealth by 0.99, giving a 1% loss. Summing the simple returns produces zero and misses compounding. This also explains why an arithmetic average return and a compound growth rate answer different questions.

Cash and excess returns

For an effective annual cash return rfannr_f^{\mathrm{ann}} and A=252A=252 assumed sessions per year, the laboratory's constant session cash return is:

rf=(1+rfann)1/A−1,xt=Rp,t−rf.r_f=(1+r_f^{\mathrm{ann}})^{1/A}-1,\qquad x_t=R_{p,t}-r_f.
(06)

The conversion preserves compound annual cash growth. Dividing the annual percentage by 252 is an approximation and uses a different convention. For real markets, cash accrual follows actual dates, day-count rules and the appropriate funding instrument. Trading-day annualization is a teaching simplification.

Uninvested capital is not automatically idle with zero return. A long/cash strategy should specify what the cash earns. A leveraged or short portfolio also needs borrowing and collateral assumptions, which can differ from the deposit rate. The main laboratory caps risky exposure at 100% and excludes borrowing and shorts to keep this distinction transparent.

Comparable benchmarks

Compare strategy and benchmark over the same eligible interval, from the same starting wealth and with stated costs. Buy-and-hold must pay its entry cost if the strategy pays entry costs. A benchmark with a longer sample includes different market episodes and cannot be directly compared by final wealth alone.

Use cash, passive market exposure and a suitably risk-matched alternative when they answer relevant questions. A lower-risk strategy can have a smaller drawdown simply because it holds less stock. Comparing it with a proportionally scaled passive allocation can help distinguish exposure reduction from timing value, while the scaling itself should be determined without evaluation-sample hindsight.

Save both return series and wealth curves. Returns support period-by-period attribution and statistics; wealth reveals compounding and path losses. Reconstructing wealth from the saved net returns is an important reconciliation check.

06 / Signals

Signal families and forecasting targets

A signal summarizes information thought to be relevant to a future return, risk or trading opportunity. Its forecasting target may be a conditional mean return, a probability of a positive move, a relative ranking or a volatility forecast. These targets require different evaluation methods. Classification accuracy alone does not determine a strategy's profitability.

μ^t,h=𝔼^[Rt,t+h|Ft],p^t,h=ℙ^(Rt,t+h>0|Ft).\widehat\mu_{t,h}=\widehat{\mathbb E}[R_{t,t+h}\mid\mathcal F_t],\qquad \widehat p_{t,h}=\widehat{\mathbb P}(R_{t,t+h}>0\mid\mathcal F_t).
(07)

A rule can predict direction correctly most of the time while losing money if its occasional errors are much larger than its gains. A ranking can identify relatively strong assets even when every asset falls. A volatility forecast can improve sizing without predicting the sign of returns. Keep the signal's target separate from the portfolio's realized objective.

Common families

Trend signals use an asset's past movement. Contrarian signals respond to deviations or recent losses. Cross-sectional signals rank assets relative to one another. Value and quality signals use economic or accounting quantities. Carry signals summarize the return associated with holding a position under specified unchanged-state assumptions. Event signals use announcements or order-flow changes.

These names cover many implementations. A futures carry strategy needs contract rolls, financing and collateral assumptions. An equity value signal needs publication dates and point-in-time accounting data. A price z-score is a standardized deviation, not an estimate of fundamental value. The economic mechanism determines which definition is meaningful.

Signal strength and position maps

Binary rules choose among states such as long or cash. Continuous rules translate signal strength into exposure, often with clipping. A smooth map can reduce abrupt changes but can still produce large turnover when features move rapidly. Combining several signals can diversify model error, provided their dependence and research-selection process are examined.

wtraw=clip(ast,−wmax,wmax).w_t^{\mathrm{raw}}=\operatorname{clip}(a s_t,-w_{\max},w_{\max}).
(08)

The coefficient aa sets sensitivity, and clipping bounds exposure. In the main laboratory the allowed range is instead zero to one, because the example excludes shorting and leverage. A negative directional signal selects cash rather than an opposite stock position.

Feature quality versus portfolio quality

Evaluate a feature before embedding it in an elaborate optimization. Inspect its temporal stability, conditional returns, turnover implications and dependence on known risk factors. Then evaluate the complete strategy with execution and costs. A strong-looking feature can fail economically after trading frictions; an apparently weak direction forecast can still be useful for reducing a particular portfolio risk.

Every feature transformation is a research choice. Lag length, winsorization, nonlinear interactions and regime filters expand the set of tested variants. Preserve the search history so that the eventual result is evaluated against the experiment actually conducted.

07 / Signals

Time-series momentum and trend filters

Time-series momentum uses an asset's own past movement. A simple formation signal compares the current close with a close LL sessions earlier:

Mt,L=PtPt−L−1,at=𝟙{Mt,L>0}.M_{t,L}=\frac{P_t}{P_{t-L}}-1,\qquad a_t=\mathbb 1_{\{M_{t,L}>0\}}.
(09)

The indicator is a long/cash signal. A long/short version would map positive and negative values to opposite positions and would need a different financing and shorting model. Cross-sectional momentum instead compares assets' past returns with each other, so it need not agree with this absolute direction rule.

Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) study time-series momentum in a broad futures dataset. The daily single-asset teaching rule here is a distinct implementation and does not reproduce that paper's instrument universe, horizon or empirical result.

Moving-average filters

A moving average smooths noisy price observations. For a window of LL price observations:

MAt,L=1L∑j=0L−1Pt−j.\operatorname{MA}_{t,L}=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}P_{t-j}.
(10)

A price-above-average rule compares PtP_t with this smoothed level. A crossover rule compares fast and slow averages. These rules are related to trend direction but differ from a trailing return: one uses an average of intervening prices, while the other compares two endpoints. A plot that overlays both should not label them as mathematically identical.

Trend persistence and whipsaw

Trend filters can benefit when price movement persists long enough for a delayed signal to participate. They can suffer in alternating markets where a signal turns positive just before reversal. The delay means the strategy usually gives up part of a move at entry and exit. That is part of its design rather than necessarily a coding mistake.

An analogy: a thermostat with a slow sensor

A smoothed trend signal resembles a thermostat averaging recent temperatures. Averaging suppresses short fluctuations, but the reading responds late when conditions change. A faster sensor reacts sooner and also changes its recommendation more often. The trade-off appears as lag versus turnover and whipsaw.

Lookback and hysteresis

Short lookbacks can react quickly but often trade more. Long lookbacks can miss rapid regime changes. A no-trade band or hysteresis can reduce repeated transitions near zero: enter when momentum exceeds a positive threshold and exit when it falls below a lower threshold. Such a rule has state and must be implemented sequentially.

The laboratory uses the simpler zero-threshold binary signal, evaluated on each formation day. It keeps no hidden hysteresis state. Optional volatility scaling changes the amount held on long days. This separation makes the effects of directional selection and risk scaling easier to inspect.

Do not select a lookback only because one sample gives it the best Sharpe ratio. Examine neighboring values, cost sensitivity, delayed execution and independent evaluation. A mechanism should normally tolerate small changes in an arbitrary measurement window better than a peak created by noise.

08 / Signals

Mean reversion and contrarian signals

A mean-reversion strategy assumes some deviation tends to decline over a specified horizon. The deviation might be a price relative to an economic anchor, a spread between related instruments or a standardized short-term move. The anchor and horizon are essential: an asset price below a moving average is not automatically below a stable equilibrium.

zt=Pt−P¯t,LsP,t,L,at=𝟙{zt<−1}.z_t=\frac{P_t-\overline P_{t,L}}{s_{P,t,L}},\qquad a_t=\mathbb 1_{\{z_t<-1\}}.
(11)

This is the laboratory's illustrative contrarian long/cash signal. The rolling mean and sample standard deviation use LL price observations ending at formation close tt. It goes long while the current z-score is below −1 and is otherwise in cash. It is not a persistent position held until a separate exit condition is met.

Normalization is not stationarity

Dividing by a rolling standard deviation makes a deviation dimensionless, but does not prove that price levels are stationary or that a low z-score predicts recovery. A declining trend can produce repeated negative deviations while continuing to fall. A moving anchor can also follow the price rather than represent an independent equilibrium.

A genuinely stationary spread may be modeled by a discrete autoregression or an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. For an OU deviation XtX_t with mean-reversion speed κ>0\kappa>0:

dXt=κ(θ−Xt)dt+σdWt,h1/2=ln2κ.dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t,\qquad h_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{\kappa}.
(12)

The half-life is a conditional expected-deviation decay measure under that model. Estimating it from a short, selected sample can be unstable. A fitted half-life is not a guarantee that a particular trade recovers within that time.

Pairs and relative value

A pairs strategy trades a spread or residual after a hedge relation is estimated. High correlation does not imply a stationary spread. Cointegration concerns a stable combination of nonstationary levels under specific statistical assumptions. Estimate hedge ratios and test relationships within the training period, then account for hedge rebalancing, short borrow and execution on both legs.

A spread's apparent mean reversion can reflect stale prices or asynchronous closes. A strategy may be buying the leg with an old mark and selling the leg whose price has already updated. A synchronized and executable data model is therefore crucial before interpreting a statistical relationship as an opportunity.

Tail behavior and stopping rules

Contrarian positions can accumulate exposure during large adverse moves. A stop-loss or maximum holding period limits a stated trading policy but changes the return distribution and must be tested as part of that policy. A stop trigger does not guarantee a fill at the trigger price; jumps and illiquidity can create larger losses.

Distinguish a statistical reversion forecast from risk control. Position caps, diversification and exit rules may be necessary even when the forecast is well motivated. A negative deviation alone is insufficient to justify unlimited averaging into a losing position.

09 / Forecasting

Feature normalization and predictive models

Features should use information available at their formation dates. Rolling standardization, volatility estimates and cross-sectional rankings can make signals comparable, but their fitting procedure must remain causal. A full-sample mean and standard deviation leak future distribution information into earlier feature rows.

x~t=xt−μ^trainσ^train,y^t=fθ^train(x~t).\widetilde x_t=\frac{x_t-\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{train}}} {\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{train}}},\qquad \widehat y_t=f_{\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{train}}}(\widetilde x_t).
(13)

Fit normalization parameters and model coefficients in the training set, then apply them unchanged during the evaluation block unless an online update rule was specified in advance. Refit them at the next scheduled training date. The same logic applies to missing-value imputation, dimensionality reduction, feature selection and target transformations.

Prediction targets and overlapping labels

A label such as the next five-session return uses observations after the feature date. That is normal for supervised learning, but the label is not available until its horizon ends. Training at date tt can include only labels already realized by tt. Adjacent five-session labels overlap, making errors and samples dependent.

A direction classifier, expected-return regression and volatility model should be scored against their own targets. Calibration matters for predicted probabilities. A model output of 0.8 should have a stated interpretation and empirical reliability, rather than being treated as a dimensionless confidence score without validation.

Forecast-to-position translation

Under a simple mean–variance decision model, a scalar exposure can be proportional to forecast expected excess return divided by forecast variance:

wtraw=μ^tγσ^t2.w_t^{\mathrm{raw}}=\frac{\widehat\mu_t}{\gamma\widehat\sigma_t^2}.
(14)

This formula assumes a particular utility approximation, horizon and definition of returns. Small variance estimates can create very large positions; practical systems cap exposure and account for estimation uncertainty, costs and constraints. A model trained to minimize forecast error is not automatically trained to maximize implementable portfolio utility.

Complexity and regularization

Regularization can reduce coefficient instability and discourage fitting noise. It does not repair data leakage or eliminate multiple-testing bias from trying many regularizers, architectures and feature sets. Compare complex models with simple baselines on the same sample and execution assumptions.

Feature importance is conditional on the model and dataset. A feature can be useful because it proxies market exposure or volatility rather than because it forecasts a tradable anomaly. Inspect economic interpretation, stability and costs, and preserve the full training pipeline rather than only its final fitted model.

10 / Risk allocation

Position sizing and volatility targeting

A directional rule specifies when to take risk. Sizing specifies how much. The laboratory combines its long/cash indicator with a backward-looking volatility estimate, using a maximum risky weight of one:

σ^tann=As(Rt−v+1,…,Rt),wttarget=atmin(1,σtargetσ^tann).\widehat\sigma_t^{\mathrm{ann}}= \sqrt A\,s(R_{t-v+1},\ldots,R_t),\qquad w_t^{\mathrm{target}}=a_t \min\!\left(1,\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}} {\widehat\sigma_t^{\mathrm{ann}}}\right).
(15)

The sample standard deviation uses vv returns and denominator v−1v-1. Inputs belong to the formation day's information set. The position is subsequently executed with the specified delay. If observed volatility is numerically zero, the laboratory uses the exposure cap rather than dividing by zero.

What the target means

A 12% volatility target is a scaling rule based on an estimate, not a promise that realized strategy volatility will be 12%. The strategy may be in cash, the cap may bind, volatility may change after formation, and estimation and execution can lag. Costs also affect realized returns.

Volatility targeting can materially change a signal's performance. It reduces exposure after high-volatility observations and increases it when estimated risk is lower, up to the cap. The effect is distinct from the directional signal and should be evaluated separately. A strategy that looks stronger after scaling may owe much of its change to risk management rather than return forecasting.

Risk limits and concentration

Other limits include gross and net exposure, single-position concentration, factor exposures, liquidity participation, drawdown rules and tail-risk budgets. A single-asset unlevered laboratory cannot demonstrate diversification; it can only show exposure modulation. Multi-asset systems require covariance or joint scenario information.

Kelly sizing maximizes expected log growth under its model. For a small-return approximation, exposure resembles expected excess return divided by variance. Parameter uncertainty, fat tails and trading constraints can make estimated full-Kelly exposures highly unstable. Fractional sizing and caps express different practical choices, rather than an exact universal optimum.

Sizing creates trading

Even if a directional signal remains long for many days, a changing volatility estimate can trigger frequent small rebalances. Turnover and costs depend on the entire position map. Count actual notional traded from the account, not only the number of signal sign changes.

A no-trade band can compare target and current drifted exposure and act only when their difference is sufficiently large. Rebalance frequency and bands should be part of the tested specification. They trade off tracking the desired risk with paying implementation costs.

11 / Portfolios

Portfolio construction and exposure constraints

In a multi-asset strategy, a collection of forecasts must be translated into jointly feasible positions. Expected return, covariance, signal reliability, trading costs and constraints all matter. The Markowitz notes derive the basic mean–variance problem; a trading implementation adds the cost of changing the existing portfolio.

maxwμ^Tw−γ2wTΣ^w−C(w−wcurrent).\max_w\ \widehat\mu^{\mathsf T}w -\frac{\gamma}{2}w^{\mathsf T}\widehat\Sigma w -\mathcal C(w-w^{\mathrm{current}}).
(16)

The current weights are the weights after market movement and before the new trade. The objective's units must be consistent: forecasts, covariance and cost penalties should refer to compatible horizons. A one-time transaction cost is not automatically comparable to an annual expected return without specifying how long the position is expected to persist.

Gross and net exposure

Net risky exposure is ∑iwi\sum_iw_i, while gross risky exposure is ∑i|wi|\sum_i|w_i|. A market-neutral portfolio can have net exposure near zero and substantial gross exposure, financing requirements and tail risk. A unit net budget does not limit leverage when large long and short positions offset each other.

Dollar neutrality does not imply factor neutrality. A long small-cap basket and a short large-cap basket can have zero net capital while retaining market beta, size and liquidity exposure. Constraints should identify the actual risks intended to be controlled, and their estimation uncertainty should be examined.

Signal combination

Equal-weighted signal portfolios are useful baselines. Optimized combinations can exploit forecast differences but can also amplify estimation noise. Diversifying model families may be more informative than combining many almost-identical lookbacks whose errors move together.

Risk contributions should be calculated for the aggregate portfolio. Summing standalone volatilities or VaRs ignores dependence. Scenario ES can provide a tail-sensitive objective when the decision and cost model permit it. The VaR and ES notes explain coherent aggregation and component tail risk.

Constrained trading

Position limits, sector bounds, minimum lots, restricted instruments and borrow availability can make the desired portfolio unattainable. Store both desired and filled holdings. A research result based only on unconstrained target weights may not describe the account that can actually be traded.

In the single-asset laboratory, risky weights lie between zero and one and the remainder is cash. The cap removes borrowing and short-position complications, while still illustrating signal timing, drifted weights, sizing and transaction costs. The simplicity is deliberate and should not be mistaken for a complete multi-asset implementation.

12 / Trading frictions

Transaction costs and turnover

A strategy earns implementable results after the costs of its trades. Commissions, bid–ask crossing, market impact, exchange fees, financing and borrow charges have different sources. A single proportional cost is a useful teaching abstraction, but should not conceal those differences when analyzing a real market.

Define one-way traded notional as the absolute amount bought or sold. If a position increases by €10,000, one-way notional is €10,000. Buying and later selling that position involves two trades and approximately €20,000 total notional before price movement. Some reports divide total buys plus sells by two and call that turnover; state the convention.

τt=|Δqt|PtEtpre,Ct=c|Δqt|Pt=cτtEtpre.\tau_t=\frac{|\Delta q_t|P_t}{E_t^{\mathrm{pre}}},\qquad C_t=c\,|\Delta q_t|P_t=c\,\tau_tE_t^{\mathrm{pre}}.
(17)

Here cc is cost as a fraction of one-way traded notional. Ten basis points means c=0.001c=0.001, because one basis point is 10−410^{-4}. The laboratory deducts this all-in amount from wealth at each trade. It does not additionally charge an implicit spread in the fill price.

Spread conventions

If a full quoted spread is ten basis points around a midpoint, a market buy crosses roughly five basis points from midpoint to ask, and a market sell crosses roughly five to bid. A round trip crosses the full spread if conditions remain unchanged. Charging the full spread on each side doubles that simplified spread cost.

If the backtest already executes at ask for buys and bid for sells, the spread is already reflected in P&L. Adding another spread deduction double counts it. Fees and impact can still be additional. Specify whether prices are midpoints, trades or executable quotes before attaching a cost assumption.

Turnover depends on drift

For a costless multi-asset rebalance, pre-trade weights drift after returns. With a compatible cash model, the risky weight of asset ii becomes:

w~i,t=wi,t−1(1+Ri,t)1+Rp,t.\widetilde w_{i,t}= \frac{w_{i,t-1}(1+R_{i,t})}{1+R_{p,t}}.
(18)

A new target should be compared with these drifted weights, not simply with yesterday's target. The difference is especially important for constant-mix portfolios. The exact laboratory additionally solves for post-cost target fractions, so fees and the denominator of wealth remain consistent.

Cost sensitivity and a break-even approximation

If average gross excess return per session is x¯gross\overline x_{\mathrm{gross}} and average one-way turnover is τ¯>0\overline\tau>0, a first-order break-even cost is:

cbreak≈x¯grossτ¯.c_{\mathrm{break}}\approx \frac{\overline x_{\mathrm{gross}}}{\overline\tau}.
(19)

This is a diagnostic approximation, not an exact compound-account identity. Financing, changing exposure, nonlinear impact and cost-dependent behavior can alter it. A negative gross excess mean has no positive cost allowance under this approximation.

Test cost ranges rather than only a convenient optimistic value. A signal with small gross advantage and high turnover has little room for execution error. When costs depend on volatility, volume or trade size, perturb those conditions as well as the average coefficient.

13 / Execution

Execution, orders and fill assumptions

A backtest needs a model of when orders are released, at what prices they can execute and what fraction fills. A closing observation is a valuation mark unless the execution model makes it an obtainable price. An assumption of guaranteed fills should be visible, especially when a strategy depends on brief or illiquid opportunities.

Market, limit and stop orders

A market order prioritizes execution but does not guarantee a price. A limit order bounds acceptable price but can remain unfilled or partially filled. A stop order defines a trigger and subsequent order behavior; a price gap can produce a fill far from the stop level. Historical bar highs and lows do not reveal the exact sequence of events inside a bar.

If a bar contains both a stop and a profit target, their execution order can change the result. Choose a justified intrabar model, use finer data or report a range. A favorable ordering chosen after seeing the bar is a form of hindsight.

Opportunity, queue and adverse selection

The figure's arrival model illustrates why waiting time changes the probability of observing an opportunity. It does not model a real limit order. Actual fills depend on displayed and hidden liquidity, queue position, cancellations, matching rules and prices. Orders may fill most often when the subsequent move is unfavorable, so estimating average spread capture without adverse selection can exaggerate results.

A limit strategy should distinguish quoted opportunity from realized filled P&L. Trades cannot be assigned solely to all historically touched prices without a fill model. Partial fills also change the portfolio's subsequent state and may leave hedges unbalanced.

Latency and market impact

Signal computation, order routing and execution all take time. For a daily strategy, an additional session of delay can test sensitivity. For intraday strategies, milliseconds or seconds may matter and demand appropriately timestamped data. A delay stress should preserve causal decisions rather than simply shift a profitable realized P&L curve.

Large orders can move prices and spread execution across time. A model such as Almgren and Chriss (2001) studies the trade-off between transaction costs and price risk during execution. Its framework requires calibrated inputs and a stated objective; it is not a universal fixed impact charge.

The teaching execution model

The laboratory executes the precomputed target at a subsequent synthetic close, in full, with a proportional all-in cost. It has no queue, bid–ask series, partial fills or market impact. Those assumptions make the ledger exact within the specified model. The execution-delay control examines one operational sensitivity while leaving the fill assumption explicit.

For live deployment, log order intent, submission time, acknowledgments, cancellations, fills and position reconciliation. Compare realized implementation shortfall with the research assumptions. Operational records are part of the strategy evidence, not merely administrative data.

14 / Account mechanics

Cash, holdings and self-financing accounting

A share-and-cash ledger is a direct way to verify a backtest. Before trading at price PP, let wealth be EE, stock value be S=qPS=qP, and cash be B=E−SB=E-S. Choose a desired risky fraction ww measured after fees. The trade should leave exactly that fraction of post-cost wealth in stock.

Let h=S/Eh=S/E be the current risky fraction and u=Snew/Eu=S_{\mathrm{new}}/E the new stock value expressed relative to pre-trade wealth. Fees are cE|u−h|cE|u-h|. The target condition is:

w=u1−c|u−h|.w=\frac{u}{1-c|u-h|}.
(20)

Solve it separately according to trade direction. If w≥hw\ge h, the transaction is a buy; if w<hw<h, it is a sell:

ubuy=w(1+ch)1+cw,usell=w(1−ch)1−cw.u_{\mathrm{buy}}=\frac{w(1+ch)}{1+cw},\qquad u_{\mathrm{sell}}=\frac{w(1-ch)}{1-cw}.
(21)

For 0≤w,h≤10\le w,h\le1 and small 0≤c<10\le c<1, the equations have valid positive denominators. The laboratory inputs use a much smaller cost range. The formulas avoid assuming that target fractions remain unchanged when fees reduce the wealth denominator.

C=cE|u−h|,Snew=Eu,Bnew=E−C−Snew.C=cE|u-h|,\qquad S_{\mathrm{new}}=Eu,\qquad B_{\mathrm{new}}=E-C-S_{\mathrm{new}}.
(22)

Holdings evolution

After the trade, shares are qnew=Snew/Pq_{\mathrm{new}}=S_{\mathrm{new}}/P. Hold them over the next price interval and accrue cash at the specified cash rate:

Enext=qnewPnext+Bnew(1+rf).E_{\mathrm{next}}=q_{\mathrm{new}}P_{\mathrm{next}} +B_{\mathrm{new}}(1+r_f).
(23)

Equivalently, if RR is the asset return and τ=|u−h|\tau=|u-h|, the account's exact one-period wealth ratio in this model is:

1+Rp=(1−cτ)[1+wR+(1−w)rf].1+R_p=(1-c\tau)\left[1+wR+(1-w)r_f\right].
(24)

The familiar approximation Rp≈wR+(1−w)rf−cτR_p\approx wR+(1-w)r_f-c\tau drops the product between the fee deduction and subsequent gross return. It is often small, but the share-and-cash ledger retains it and reconciles exactly.

Entry and exit examples

Starting with €100 in cash, target w=1w=1 and cost 10 bps, new stock value is 100/1.001≈99.90010100/1.001\approx99.90010, with fee about 0.09990 and zero remaining cash. Buying €100 of stock and then deducting a separate fee would create negative cash and accidental borrowing.

Starting entirely in stock and targeting zero, sell the stock, deduct the fee and retain the remainder in cash. If the price fell before exit, that loss belongs to the holding interval before the trade. The target calculation must use the actual current stock value rather than the original investment amount.

Reconciliation checks

At each event, verify stock plus cash equals wealth, post-cost exposure equals the target, fees equal the stated cost times traded notional, and the next wealth equals revalued shares plus accrued cash. Reconstruct final wealth by multiplying saved net return factors. The checks are complementary and can locate errors in sizing, cash treatment or return attribution.

15 / Implementation

Backtest engines and event ordering

A backtest engine simulates a decision policy under a market and execution model. A vectorized implementation can be efficient for simple rules, while an event-driven implementation is often clearer when orders, partial fills and state matter. Correct event ordering is more important than the programming style.

A daily event sequence

  1. Read the already-known target whose execution time has arrived.
  2. Value current shares and cash at the rebalance mark.
  3. Calculate the trade, charge its cost and update holdings.
  4. Hold shares through the next price interval and accrue cash.
  5. Save net return, wealth, exposure, trade notional and fee.
  6. Observe the new closing data and form targets for later execution.

Formation can be precomputed when it depends only on past data and its causality is verified. State-dependent rules require sequential computation: a stop, holding-period cap or hysteresis transition depends on earlier account decisions. Replacing such a rule with a stateless boolean array changes the strategy.

Warm-up and common evaluation

A 63-session trailing return first exists at close 63. With one-session execution delay, it is executed at close 64 and first affects the return ending on day 65. The benchmark study therefore starts every wealth curve at close 64. A volatility window can extend warm-up if it requires more observations than the signal.

Changing a lookback can change the first eligible date. For cross-parameter comparisons, use a common evaluation start after the longest required warm-up. The robustness study does so. Within the laboratory, the strategy and its benchmarks always share the start implied by the current inputs; comparing separate laboratory runs still requires checking their displayed start and period count.

Gross and net accounts

A zero-cost account is rerun with the same signals and sizing, rather than constructed by adding cumulative fees to final net wealth. Fees change the capital available to compound. Gross-minus-net wealth therefore differs from the arithmetic sum of fee payments.

Do not silently omit the first purchase or require a final liquidation only for the strategy. The main comparison values both strategy and benchmark at the final mark without forced liquidation. A realized exit analysis can instead liquidate both and charge the applicable final cost, but it answers a slightly different accounting question.

Implementation verification

Use deterministic miniature paths that can be calculated by hand. Test all-cash, all-stock, unchanged targets, fractional weights, zero cost and nonzero cash return. Compare an optimized engine with an independently written holdings ledger. Perturb future prices to test causality. Such checks verify the computation within its assumptions; they do not establish market predictability.

Store model configuration, seed or data snapshot, code version and event records. A final wealth chart alone contains too little information to reconstruct why a strategy traded or to diagnose a disagreement between implementations.

16 / Evaluation design

Training, validation and evaluation samples

Divide the research process into fitting, model selection and final evaluation. Training estimates coefficients or constructs a rule. Validation compares permitted choices. A final evaluation assesses the selected procedure on observations not used to choose it. In time-series applications, these roles usually need a chronological information boundary.

training⟶validation⟶evaluation.\text{training}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{validation}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{evaluation}.
(25)

The arrows represent availability, not a universal ratio of sample sizes. A five-year dataset and a five-decade dataset support different choices. The strategy horizon, regime variability and number of variants determine how much evidence each stage can provide.

Chronological separation

Randomly shuffling dated rows can put future regimes and overlapping return labels into training before they are evaluated. A chronological split better represents a prospective forecasting problem. Temporal separation alone is insufficient if preprocessing, universe membership or labels still contain future information.

Use earlier observations to initialize rolling features at the beginning of an evaluation block. Those historical observations are not leakage simply because they precede the block. What must remain unavailable is the block's later outcomes when fitting the decision that acts at its start.

Nested model selection

If hyperparameters are tuned, use an inner training/validation process inside each outer training period. Score the selected process on the outer evaluation block. Training a model repeatedly on one validation period eventually adapts it to that period, even if the model never directly includes those labels in its fitting objective.

The complete selection procedure is the object being evaluated. Choosing the best rule once using all history and then drawing chronological folds does not undo that earlier selection. Define candidate lists and selection criteria before the folds' outcomes are examined.

Benchmarks and costs belong inside selection

A parameter chosen using gross returns can favor a high-turnover rule that fails after costs. If implementable net performance is the stated objective, apply the cost model during selection. Likewise, a risk-adjusted selection metric must use the same cash and return conventions as evaluation.

Sample dependence and small counts can make validation rankings unstable. Preserve alternative near-ties and examine stability rather than treating an estimated maximum as a known optimum. A simple rule with a broad robust neighborhood can be more credible than a complex winner whose ranking changes after one observation.

Evaluation is consumed by feedback

Once a final period's result drives changes to features or parameters, that period becomes part of development. Keeping its label “test” does not restore independence. Obtain genuinely new observations or report that evaluation is exploratory. The synthetic examples here remain demonstrations even when their event timing is causal.

17 / Prospective simulation

Walk-forward selection and stitched returns

A walk-forward procedure repeatedly fits or selects a rule from past observations and deploys it on subsequent intervals. A rolling window keeps a fixed-length history; an expanding window retains all eligible past data. Each design changes the trade-off between adaptation and sample size.

θ^k=argmaxθ∈ΘJ(θ;Dtrain,k),Reval,k=B(θ^k;Dfuture,k).\widehat\theta_k=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta} J(\theta;\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train},k}),\qquad R_{\mathrm{eval},k}=\mathcal B(\widehat\theta_k;\mathcal D_{\mathrm{future},k}).
(26)

The objective JJ, candidate set Θ\Theta and fitting schedule must be specified in advance. The backtest operator B\mathcal B includes execution and account state, not merely the future returns multiplied by an ideal target.

The computed example

The study compares lookbacks 21, 42, 63, 126 and 252 sessions. It selects the highest net training Sharpe using up to 504 earlier sessions and refits every 126 sessions. Every candidate is evaluated over the same eligible training interval, beginning no earlier than close 253. There is no volatility scaling in this example, so selection concerns the directional lookback.

The first fit is completed after close 504. Because the selected signal is formed then and executed one session later, it first affects return 506. Return 505 is still earned under the predeployment cash state. At later refits, the previous deployed rule continues until the new target becomes executable; there is no artificial block-boundary cash reset.

Stitching an account

Continue shares and cash across evaluation blocks, including the costs of changing selected rules. Concatenating independently normalized block equity curves can hide entry, exit and transition costs. Concatenating valid block return series is acceptable only if their initial holdings and transitions represent the continuous trading policy.

A portfolio already holding stock at a parameter switch may need to sell part or all of it. That trade is part of the walk-forward outcome. The training simulations begin from a common account convention for scoring, while the deployed evaluation ledger carries its actual state forward.

What walk-forward establishes

Past-only fitting avoids one class of look-ahead and approximates a prospective decision process. It does not eliminate a researcher's selection among several walk-forward schedules, cost assumptions or candidate sets. Testing many procedures and reporting the best still creates selection bias.

Regime coverage also matters. A procedure that succeeds during one long trend may fail in a different market structure. Evaluate distributions of block outcomes, selected-parameter stability, exposure and turnover. A stitched line can look smooth while hiding that nearly all performance came from one block.

The plotted synthetic result should be interpreted as a demonstration of the procedure and its timing. It supplies no independent empirical evidence about real assets. That evidence would require a point-in-time dataset and a research process whose choices were fixed before evaluation.

18 / Validation mechanics

Overlapping labels, purging and embargoes

Many prediction labels cover an interval. A feature at close tt might predict the return through close t+5t+5. Adjacent labels then share price observations. A validation boundary at date tt does not imply that every training label whose feature date is earlier than tt has already finished.

Yt=Pt+hPt−1,label interval [t,t+h].Y_t=\frac{P_{t+h}}{P_t}-1,\qquad \text{label interval }[t,t+h].
(27)

When fitting after close bb, include this label only if its endpoint is no later than bb. In a simple chronological split, dropping unfinished training labels at the boundary is necessary to avoid future outcomes entering the fit.

Purging interval overlap

Purging removes training examples whose outcome intervals overlap the evaluation outcome intervals under the chosen validation design. Event-based labels can have varying endpoints, so purging should use actual intervals rather than an arbitrary fixed number of rows. Feature windows can introduce additional dependence that needs separate consideration.

For example, a label starting on day 98 and ending on day 103 overlaps an evaluation interval beginning on day 100. It must not be treated as a completed past label at the day-100 boundary. The earlier feature timestamp alone does not make it available.

Embargoes and dependence

An embargo leaves a gap around or after evaluation regions to reduce information spillover in a specified resampling scheme. Its length should reflect label horizons, feature memory and dependence. It is not a magic fixed percentage that makes any dataset independent. A gap that is too short leaves overlap; one that is too long discards useful information without necessarily addressing the real leakage mechanism.

In pure walk-forward testing, future training rows are excluded by construction. Purging unfinished labels at each fit still matters. In folds that train on observations both before and after a held-out block, additional overlap and temporal-information questions arise. Such cross-validation estimates are not automatically equivalent to a real-time trading deployment.

Boundaries in the teaching study

The walk-forward example scores completed one-session account returns and selects only after the training close. It adds execution latency before deployment. It does not train on multi-session predictive labels, so it does not implement a generalized purged machine-learning pipeline. This distinction keeps the numerical experiment aligned with its claims.

When extending it to a forecast model, save feature timestamps, label start and endpoint, fitting timestamps and the exact split membership. Check availability of every fitted target. A statement that “cross-validation was used” is too broad to establish valid temporal information flow.

19 / Research integrity

Research biases and misleading backtests

Backtest credibility depends on how observations and choices entered the experiment. Common biases are not merely statistical technicalities: they can change the direction and magnitude of apparent performance.

Look-ahead and survivorship

Look-ahead uses future information in earlier decisions. Survivorship uses a future-conditioned universe, such as current index members, at past dates. Delisting omissions, revised fundamentals and retrospective instrument selection can combine the two. A causally indexed signal cannot repair a biased universe.

Data snooping and selective reporting

Trying many indicators, windows, markets, subperiods and exits increases the chance of finding a favorable sample result. Reporting only the successful variants hides the relevant trial count. Choosing the date range after observing where the curve rises is another strategy-selection step, even if the trading rule itself remains unchanged.

Outlier removal can be legitimate when correcting a documented data error, but excluding extreme losses because they look inconvenient changes the economic sample. Distinguish vendor errors from real adverse events. A crisis observation is often exactly the event that should inform a risk assessment.

Accounting and benchmark distortions

Zero cash return can understate a cash benchmark while making low-exposure strategies easier to compare favorably. Ignoring financing can exaggerate leveraged returns. Omitting initial trades reduces costs. Summing returns instead of compounding misstates wealth. Comparing different sample intervals confounds rule differences with market-period differences.

A high win rate can coexist with poor returns. A smooth curve can come from stale pricing. A high Sharpe can come from short optionality or omitted tail events. A low drawdown can come from lower exposure rather than useful timing. Each metric needs a mechanism-aware interpretation.

Execution assumptions

Perfect limit fills, favorable intrabar order, trading at stale marks and ignoring size can create gains that disappear in realistic execution. An asset's closing price does not prove that an arbitrarily large order could have filled at that price. A research model should expose the assumptions, then test sensitivity where they matter.

A bias audit as part of research

Trace a representative trade from raw timestamped data to feature, target, order, fill, cash movement and attributed return. Record every sample exclusion and parameter choice. Preserve negative results and compare an independently implemented engine. This makes the analysis inspectable without substituting a generic checklist for actual evidence.

A backtest can be useful even when imperfect, if its limitations and experiment are stated precisely. The problem is interpreting a simulation under favorable assumptions as stronger evidence than it actually provides.

20 / Statistical selection

Multiple testing and backtest overfitting

If each independent null strategy has a false-positive probability pp, testing MM strategies gives probability of at least one false positive:

ℙ(at least one false positive)=1−(1−p)M.\mathbb P(\text{at least one false positive})=1-(1-p)^M.
(28)

At p=5%p=5\% and M=20M=20, the probability is about 64.15%. Real strategy trials are often correlated, so this independent formula is an illustration rather than a universal calibration. The basic issue remains: choosing a sample maximum changes the distribution of the reported statistic.

The winner's advantage can be noise

The figure simulates candidate return series with zero true mean. The best in-sample Sharpe grows as more candidates are searched, while independently evaluated performance remains centered near zero. No candidate acquires predictive ability because it won the training competition. The gap is selection optimism under the toy null.

Parameter neighborhoods, feature transformations and research restarts are all trials when they can influence the reported winner. Correlated candidates reduce the amount of independent variation, but counting only the final number of published rules severely understates the search in many workflows.

Statistical approaches

Multiple-testing procedures control different error criteria. Family-wise methods target the probability of any false rejection in a family; false-discovery-rate methods target the expected proportion of false discoveries among rejections under their assumptions. Bootstrap reality-check methods can account for searching a strategy family relative to a benchmark. White (2000) develops a data-snooping reality check.

Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) study multiple testing in the cross-section of expected returns. Their setting differs from this daily strategy laboratory, but the lesson about ordinary significance thresholds after broad searches is directly relevant. A threshold derived for one experiment should not be transplanted mechanically to another.

PBO and deflated performance

The probability-of-backtest-overfitting framework of Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu examines how in-sample selection can translate into poor relative out-of-sample ranking across structured splits. A PBO estimate depends on the strategy family, statistic and resampling scheme; it is not the probability that a particular live account will lose money.

The deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts a performance assessment for selection and non-normality under a stated approximation. Its inputs include information about trials and their dependence. It cannot recover an unrecorded research history or make unreliable prices tradable.

Keep a complete experiment log, reserve genuinely new evaluation data and use economically motivated, limited candidate sets. Statistical corrections help quantify a search's consequences; they complement research discipline rather than replace it.

21 / Performance

Performance statistics and benchmark comparisons

Performance evaluation should use a collection of interpretable statistics on a reconciled net return series. No single ratio describes growth, risk, tails, timing and implementation. State the sample length and annualization convention alongside the metrics.

Growth and dispersion

For TT observed return periods and AA periods per modeled year, total return and compound annual growth rate are:

Rtotal=ETE0−1,CAGR=(ETE0)A/T−1.R_{\mathrm{total}}=\frac{E_T}{E_0}-1,\qquad \operatorname{CAGR}=\left(\frac{E_T}{E_0}\right)^{A/T}-1.
(29)

CAGR is the constant compound annual rate that reaches the same endpoint under the stated time convention. It does not describe the path between endpoints. For real dates, a calendar-year exponent can be preferable to an assumed count of trading sessions.

σ^ann=A1T−1∑t=1T(Rp,t−R¯p)2.\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{ann}}=\sqrt A \sqrt{\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(R_{p,t}-\overline R_p)^2}.
(30)

This is a conventional volatility annualization. Its exact aggregation interpretation depends on return dependence and the approximation being used. The daily sample standard deviation remains a valid descriptive statistic even when the square-root annualization is not an exact model of yearly returns.

Risk-adjusted and active performance

The Sharpe ratio compares differential returns with their variability. With cash as the benchmark, define excess returns xt=Rp,t−rf,tx_t=R_{p,t}-r_{f,t}. The conventional annualized estimate is:

S^ann=Ax¯sx.\widehat S_{\mathrm{ann}}= \sqrt A\,\frac{\overline x}{s_x}.
(31)

Use the standard deviation of differential returns, not automatically the strategy's own return standard deviation when the benchmark changes over time. Sharpe (1994) discusses differential-return measurement. A zero-volatility cash account has no defined excess-return Sharpe in this convention; report it as unavailable rather than zero or infinity.

For an active strategy versus a risky benchmark, the information ratio uses mean active return divided by tracking error. It answers a different question from cash-excess Sharpe. A strategy's regression alpha depends on the factor benchmark and estimation assumptions; a positive raw return does not establish positive alpha.

Downside and trade-level statistics

The laboratory computes a Sortino-style quantity in its engine using all-period downside semideviation relative to cash:

Sortinoann=Ax¯T−1∑tmin(xt,0)2.\operatorname{Sortino}_{\mathrm{ann}}= \sqrt A\,\frac{\overline x} {\sqrt{T^{-1}\sum_t\min(x_t,0)^2}}.
(32)

Some definitions divide by only the number of downside observations; that changes the result. State the target and denominator. A denominator of zero means the ratio is unavailable under this definition, not evidence of risklessness.

Win rate, average win, average loss, trade duration and profit factor can illuminate a trading mechanism, but trade definitions matter. Frequent partial rebalances do not correspond to independent round trips. The laboratory reports nonzero rebalance orders and actual notional turnover, without calling each order a new completed trade.

Compare net growth, exposure, drawdown and turnover with the benchmark. An account can have a positive total return and still have a negative estimated excess-return Sharpe when cash earns more. The metrics summarize different aspects of the same observations.

22 / Statistical inference

Sharpe ratios, dependence and inference

An estimated Sharpe ratio is uncertain. It is a ratio of an estimated mean and standard deviation, both affected by the return-generating process. Serial dependence, skewness, heavy tails and model selection influence how much evidence a high sample value provides.

Why square-root scaling needs assumptions

For stationary additive differential returns with lag-kk autocorrelation ρk\rho_k, the standard deviation of a qq-period sum depends on all relevant autocorrelations. Its Sharpe ratio is related to the one-period ratio by:

Sq=S1q1+2∑k=1q−1(1−k/q)ρk.S_q=S_1\sqrt{\frac{q} {1+2\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}(1-k/q)\rho_k}}.
(33)

The expression assumes a stationary mean and covariance structure and refers to additive differential returns. It is not an exact formula for compounding a leveraged trading account. Under zero autocorrelation it reduces to q\sqrt q; positive dependence can make the naive multiplier too large. Lo (2002) develops Sharpe-ratio statistics and aggregation under several return-process assumptions.

Mean-return inference

Under IID returns with finite variance, the usual mean-return t-statistic is x¯/(sx/T)\overline x/(s_x/\sqrt T), equal to the sample daily Sharpe times T\sqrt T. Serial dependence requires a different standard error. A heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent estimate can use:

Ω^=γ^0+2∑k=1b(1−kb+1)γ^k,SE(x¯)≈Ω^/T.\widehat\Omega= \widehat\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{b} \left(1-\frac{k}{b+1}\right)\widehat\gamma_k,\qquad \operatorname{SE}(\overline x)\approx\sqrt{\widehat\Omega/T}.
(34)

The autocovariances and bandwidth bb are estimation choices. This Bartlett-weighted form addresses dependence under regularity conditions. It does not repair a selected winner's distribution or make a heavy-tailed infinite-variance process obey ordinary asymptotics.

A probabilistic Sharpe approximation

A commonly used moment-based approximation evaluates whether a per-period Sharpe exceeds a reference S*S^*:

PSR(S*)≈Φ((S^−S*)T−11−γ^3S^+γ^4−14S^2).\operatorname{PSR}(S^*)\approx\Phi\!\left( \frac{(\widehat S-S^*)\sqrt{T-1}} {\sqrt{1-\widehat\gamma_3\widehat S+ \frac{\widehat\gamma_4-1}{4}\widehat S^2}}\right).
(35)

Here γ^3\widehat\gamma_3 is skewness and γ^4\widehat\gamma_4 is ordinary kurtosis, so a normal distribution has kurtosis three. The Sharpe inputs use per-period units. Substituting an annualized Sharpe while retaining the same daily TT is a unit error. This asymptotic approximation also needs appropriate moment and sampling assumptions.

Bailey and López de Prado (2014) develop deflated assessment using a selection-adjusted reference. The reference, trial dependence and non-normality assumptions matter. A high unadjusted probabilistic statistic for the winner of a large search is not automatically a valid post-selection result.

Interpretation

A p-value is a probability of data or a statistic under a specified null, not the probability that the strategy is false. A confidence interval describes repeated-sample coverage under assumptions; it does not include every possible market-model change. Report effect size, sampling support and selection history together.

The laboratory displays the conventional annualized sample Sharpe as a descriptive quantity and explicitly labels its IID scaling convention. It does not issue a trading recommendation or a significance verdict from that ratio.

23 / Risk assessment

Drawdowns, tail losses and path risk

Drawdown measures wealth relative to its own earlier high-water mark. It captures path risk that the final return and volatility can miss:

Ht=max0≤u≤tEu,Dt=EtHt−1≤0,MDDsigned=mintDt.H_t=\max_{0\le u\le t}E_u,\qquad D_t=\frac{E_t}{H_t}-1\le0,\qquad \operatorname{MDD}_{\mathrm{signed}}=\min_tD_t.
(36)

Some reports display maximum drawdown as the positive magnitude −mintDt-\min_tD_t. This guide's curves and tables use the signed convention. Including initial wealth ensures that an entry fee or immediate first-period loss is not omitted from the drawdown calculation.

Depth, duration and recovery

A drawdown can be shallow but persist for a long time, or deep and recover quickly. Duration measures time below a previous peak; recovery time measures the interval until that peak is exceeded or regained under a stated convention. An unrecovered drawdown at sample end is censored, rather than evidence of a completed recovery.

A 20% drawdown requires a 25% gain to return to the peak, because 1/(1−0.20)−1=0.251/(1-0.20)-1=0.25. Equal percentage losses and gains do not offset. Exposure changes after a loss can also slow recovery even if they reduce subsequent risk.

Tail risk and optionality

Historical VaR and ES of net period losses describe a specified one-period tail. Maximum drawdown instead depends on the sequence of returns and the sample length. Rearranging the same return observations can preserve their empirical distribution while changing drawdown substantially.

Short-option strategies can have many small gains and occasional large losses. A high hit rate and smooth short sample may conceal that asymmetry. Inspect skewness, tail scenarios, nonlinear exposure and margin requirements. The tail-risk notes explain why a quantile alone cannot describe loss severity beyond its boundary.

Risk controls and their consequences

A drawdown limit or stop changes the strategy policy. It can reduce some adverse paths and also lock in losses or miss a rebound. Evaluate the rule prospectively with executable fill assumptions. A stop threshold is a decision point, not a guaranteed loss cap.

Stress paths should include gaps, volatility increases, liquidity deterioration and operational delay where relevant. A strategy that reduces exposure after volatility rises can still experience the initial shock at its previous exposure. Backward-looking risk estimates cannot anticipate every discontinuity.

Comparability

Maximum drawdown generally changes with sample length and the regimes observed. Comparing a ten-year drawdown with a one-year drawdown without context is misleading. Use aligned intervals and examine multiple paths or blocks when assessing uncertainty. A observed maximum is a sample outcome, not a bound on future losses.

24 / Robustness

Robustness, resampling and stress experiments

A robust strategy result survives relevant perturbations without depending entirely on one arbitrary setting or unusual episode. Examine nearby lookbacks, signal thresholds, execution delays, costs, risk targets, instruments and periods. The goal is to understand sensitivity, not to search until another favorable peak appears.

Parameter neighborhoods

A broad region with similar behavior is easier to reconcile with a stable mechanism than a single isolated winning parameter. But a smooth surface can still result from a shared biased dataset or a common market exposure. Sensitivity is evidence about the implementation and sample, not proof of a persistent real-market premium.

The figure compares several costs over a common start after the longest lookback warm-up. Without a common start, longer windows omit more early returns and can appear better because they were evaluated in a different market period. This seemingly simple sample-alignment issue affects many parameter searches.

Resampling returns

An IID bootstrap reshuffles individual return observations. A block bootstrap preserves some local dependence by resampling contiguous groups. The computed example uses circular blocks of 20 sessions from the realized net strategy return series.

This experiment conditions on the realized strategy returns. It does not regenerate prices, rerun signals or repeat the researcher's parameter search. It therefore describes uncertainty in resampled paths under that return-resampling model, rather than the full uncertainty of strategy discovery and deployment.

Rerunning a decision policy

To study how a strategy responds to new market paths, simulate or resample appropriate market inputs and rerun the entire decision process. Re-estimate features and parameters according to the stated schedule. Respect multivariate dependence and corporate actions. A synthetic path must remain consistent with the strategy's required data fields.

For research-selection uncertainty, repeat selection inside each resampling or simulation experiment. Holding the winning parameter fixed understates the variation associated with choosing it. Conversely, always re-optimizing on the resampled evaluation outcome introduces hindsight rather than representing prospective selection.

Stress experiments and falsification

Increase costs, delay fills, remove a dominant profitable episode, perturb signals and compare alternative market regimes. Removing an episode is a diagnostic, not permission to delete it from the final reported sample. If a mechanism depends on a particular market condition, identify that condition before observing which exclusions improve the result.

Negative-control signals, randomized timing and simple passive baselines can reveal coding errors or ordinary exposure masquerading as predictability. A useful robustness report explains why a result changes, including unfavorable changes, rather than displaying only variants that remain profitable.

25 / Economic implementation

Attribution, capacity and forward monitoring

Attribute returns to their sources before interpreting the total. For a long/cash strategy, risky returns, cash carry, execution costs and changing exposure all contribute. An account can reduce losses mainly by holding less stock, rather than by accurately forecasting adverse days.

Exposure and timing

Compare average risky exposure with realized market exposure and performance during rising and falling periods. A regression can summarize covariance with market returns, but a dynamic strategy's conditional exposure need not be constant. Report turnover and the risk-scaling contribution beside any estimated alpha.

Separate directional selection from volatility scaling by rerunning an otherwise identical unscaled account on a common interval. Separate costs by rerunning a zero-cost account. These controlled comparisons change one component at a time; they are more interpretable than changing several rules and attributing all improvement to the signal.

Cumulative nominal fees do not equal the gross-minus-net wealth gap. Lost capital would have participated in later gains and losses. The gap also reflects that different capital bases create different currency trades under the same target fractions. Save period-by-period fees and account returns to keep the economic decomposition clear.

Capacity and market impact

Proportional-cost laboratory results scale linearly with initial capital: doubling capital doubles holdings, fees and wealth while preserving return percentages. Real costs may grow with trade size, available liquidity and participation. A strategy's capacity is the capital range over which implementation remains acceptable under a calibrated execution model.

impact(Q)≈ησ|Q|V,\operatorname{impact}(Q)\approx\eta\,\sigma \sqrt{\frac{|Q|}{V}},
(37)

This square-root form is an illustrative model, with trade size QQ, compatible traded volume VV, volatility σ\sigma and coefficient η\eta. The volume horizon and units must match. It is not a universal law or a substitute for measured execution outcomes.

Capacity can also be constrained by borrow, contract limits, crowding, inventory or signal decay. A slow execution schedule may reduce impact while losing the forecast opportunity. The trade-off belongs to the strategy's economic design.

Forward monitoring

Paper trading and a controlled forward process compare forecast assumptions with new observations. Monitor data integrity, missing inputs, exposure, turnover, actual fills, costs, risk and performance. Reconcile intended positions with actual holdings and define how stale data or rejected orders are handled.

Set review criteria before observing a disappointing month. A statistical model can experience normal variation, while a market change can also invalidate its premise. Diagnostics should distinguish execution failures, data problems, exposure changes and forecast degradation. Updating a model creates a new version whose subsequent evidence should remain traceable.

A strategy is a continuing decision system. Its research case, account mechanics and operational monitoring should tell the same story about what it does and under which assumptions it is expected to be useful.

26 / Numerical study

Interactive systematic-strategy laboratory

The laboratory runs the specified long/cash strategy on a reproducible synthetic price path. It generates market observations, forms trailing signals, optionally scales them by estimated volatility, delays execution and reconciles shares and cash after proportional costs. The same market and eligible interval are used for all displayed account comparisons.
